1.he: הזכיר הרב ז"ל מה שהוא ידע
1.note: Literally "mentioned what he knew". The verb הזכיר is also used for pronouncing a divine Name, and the tellers probably mean that he uttered a holy Name to calm the river; the text says no more.

2.note: The name may be read Pereira or Ferreira; the man is not identified here. חצר is literally "courtyard", here the house or compound. נ"ע = נוחו עדן, "may he rest in Eden", so he was dead when the story was printed.

3.note: So printed (checked on the scan): the friend asked for three numbers (שלשה נומירוס), but the note held "the five numbers". In the lotto of the time (the Genoese type, played in Italy) five numbers were drawn out of ninety, and a bet on three of them (a terno) was common; so the story may mean that the Ḥida wrote all five numbers of the draw. נומירוס is Italian/Spanish numeros; לוטיריאה is the lottery (Italian lotteria).

4.note: A letter of recommendation (Italian raccomandazione, Spanish recomendación). Letters of this kind from a known rabbi were what an emissary showed to communities to get their help; here the man wanted to collect for himself.

5.note: Literally "the hint that hints at the Aram (ארם)". The words are printed with abbreviation marks, perhaps only to mark a rhyme or a play on words; ארם may stand for האדם, "the man". Translated by the sense; not certain.

6.note: Wrapped himself in the cloak of a scholar (תלמיד חכם), i.e. passed himself off as a scholar. The Talmud condemns one who puts on the cloak of a scholar and is not a scholar (b. Bava Batra 98a).

7.note: From the Aramaic saying חכימא ברמיזא, "to the wise, by a hint": a sage who understands a hint without more words.

8.he: כלי ריקם שלא נמצא בימי אלישע
8.note: In 2 Kgs 4:1–7 the widow's oil kept flowing as long as there were empty vessels to fill: "there is not a vessel more. And the oil stopped" [2 Kgs 4:6]. Had this man been there, there would have been one more empty vessel, and the oil would not have stopped: a praise on the surface, "an empty vessel" (an ignoramus) underneath.

9.note: Aramaic phrases of Talmudic style: סאני שומעניה "his reputation was bad" (as of a scholar in b. Mo'ed Katan 17a), מרננים אבתריה "they murmured behind him".

10.note: Ḥemdat Yamim ("Delight of Days"), an anonymous kabbalistic book of customs and prayers for the Sabbath, festivals and fasts, first printed in Izmir in 1731–32. Jacob Emden and other rabbis, chiefly in Germany and Central Europe, held it to be a work of followers of Shabbetai Ẓevi (some attributed it to Nathan of Gaza), and it was suspect among Ashkenazi rabbis; it remained popular among Sephardim. So the charge that the Ḥida studied it mainly was an accusation of Sabbatian sympathies.

11.he: אם אני אהבתי חמדת ימים. השליח הנז' אהב חמדת לילות
11.note: Wordplay on the title: "Delight of Days" against "Delight of Nights". The Ḥida implies that the emissary loved the pleasures of the night, that is, women or debauchery, in keeping with the bad reputation he had. The sense of the hint is the translator's reading; the text does not spell it out.

12.note: "Was secluded": the technical term of the law of the suspected wife (sotah, Num 5:13; m. Sotah 1:2). A wife who, after her husband's warning, was alone with another man is forbidden to her husband until the ordeal of the bitter water, which, the Mishnah says, was stopped already in Second Temple times (m. Sotah 9:9). The wife of a kohen who had relations with another man is forbidden to him in any case, which is why the Ḥida rules that he must divorce her; the judges object that there were no witnesses.
